_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Mathematics unit lecture film, Fair Shares. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own order (equal parts first; top and bottom number; a fraction of a group; a fraction of an amount; same size, different name; more than one whole), and every number is the lesson page's own: 12 apples shared between 4, half of 8, 20 shillings and a quarter, 12 eggs and three quarters, one half = two quarters, four quarters = one whole, five quarters = one whole and one quarter. The whole film turns on one thing: a share is only fair when the groups hold the same number, so every group drawn here is built from one list, three to a group, and can hold no other number.
title: Fair Shares
subtitle: Grade 2 Mathematics
objectives: Understand that an object or shape can be split into four equal parts or four unequal parts.
Understand that a quarter can describe one of four equal parts of a quantity or set of objects.
Understand that one half and one quarter can be interpreted as division.
Understand that fractions (half, quarter and three-quarters) can act as operators.
Recognise the relative size of 4 , , and 1, and the equivalence of and , and , and 1.
Understand and visualise that wholes, halves and quarters can be combined to create new fractions.

beats.say: You cut a sandwich into two parts. They must be the same size.
Fair means the two pieces are equal. That is a fraction.
Here is a paper bar. Cut it into four parts.
These four parts are all the same size. They are quarters.
Now look at this bar. One piece is much wider than the others.
Four pieces, but not equal. So not one of them is a quarter.
A fraction has two numbers. Here is three quarters.
The bottom number is four. The whole is cut into four equal parts.
The top number is three. That is how many parts you take.
So shade three of the four parts. Three quarters.
A fraction can be part of a group of things.
Here are twelve apples. Share them between four children.
One each, round and round, until they are all gone.
Everyone gets three apples. None is left over.
One share out of four is a quarter. A quarter of twelve is three.

at.quarter: A quarter of twelve is three

beats.say: Half is the same idea. Eight sweets shared between two is four each.
Amina has twenty shillings. She spends a quarter of it.
Twenty shared between four is five. She spends five shillings.
There are twelve eggs. Three quarters of them are brown.
A quarter of twelve is three. So three quarters is nine.

at.qtr: A quarter of twelve is three

beats.say: Two fractions can be worth exactly the same amount.
Here is one half of the bar. Under it are two quarters.
They reach the same place. One half is two quarters.
Two quarters has bigger numbers. It is not a bigger amount.
And one half is bigger than one quarter. More pieces, smaller pieces.

at.halfbig: one half is bigger than one quarter

beats.say: Put quarters together and you just count the parts.
One quarter and two quarters make three quarters.
The bottom number stays four. The pieces are still quarters.
Four quarters fill the whole pizza. That is one whole.
Add one more quarter. Five quarters is one whole and one quarter.
A fair share is an equal share. Always check the parts.

at.fair: A fair share is an equal share

beats.say: The bottom number counts the parts. The top counts the ones you take.
A quarter of twelve is three. Two quarters is one half.
Four quarters make one whole. Now go and share something fairly.
